items.question: How do you envision an interface for designing molecules with Chai?
items.object: An interface for designing molecules with Chai
items.answer: To me, it looks a lot less like a ChatGPT and a lot more like Autodesk or SolidWorks or Figma, if you've used those things where you can kind of load up your molecule. items.question: Why did you think the time was right for Chai to pursue general models for protein design?
items.object: Chai's decision to pursue general models for protein design
items.answer: People tried this play for a while, and I think the models just really weren't there yet. Even for us, we were taking a risk in the very beginning. We were kind of banking on the models getting there. I had seen early signs of life in my work, and our CEO Josh, he was on the original ESM papers on that team at Meta, and he was seeing pretty early signs of life that there might be scaling laws here. I think we'll actually be able to start designing things. Structure prediction is getting really good. One crazy thought is we didn't have a multimer structure prediction model until 2021. That was five years ago when we could start with deep learning to actually predict the shape of two proteins at once. AlphaFold 2 was this huge breakthrough. But then AlphaFold 2 Multimer came out a year later. You really kind of needed that to unlock design in the first place anyway. We weren't even trying to predict multiple proteins at once. Around that time inverse folding kind of started working and was like, oh, protein, this actually works in the lab. Credit to the Baker lab for doing all this really excellent lab validation on all their models, but I think we're starting to see them do interesting things and actually work on real-world experiments. Now is probably the time to start betting on this. Before then, maybe you could take some experimental data from a campaign on this one target that you had and you care about, and you might be able to make some progress on that and keep hill climbing in this one very specific case. General models weren't really a thing back then. We took that bet pretty seriously and decided to push as hard as possible and really shoot for generality in our approach.

items.question: How did you approach testing whether Chai 2 could design antibodies at scale?
items.object: Chai 2's antibody design validation and selection of 50 targets
items.answer: When Chai 2 came out, our second paper after Chai 1, we showed the world this is actually possible and it's possible at scale. We didn't show this for one or two targets; we were like, let's just go all in. Josh likes to say we set a bold companywide challenge to design antibodies to 50 targets, and we saw some signs of life. We were like, all right, let's do this with real statistics and see if this actually works. It's an interesting story of how we chose these targets. We were like, all right, what targets are we going to choose? We should choose some interesting targets, whatever. At that point we were ramping up with CROs and figuring out what our wet lab process looks like. After trying some stuff with many proteins, we were like, here are the interesting targets. This is what we should look at. Half the time the targets just kind of didn't work. We were still learning, and we were like, all right, maybe we should just go with targets that the CRO had actually validated. So let's get the CRO catalog, see what they've already worked on, restrict that to an interesting set. From that we chose 50 targets, designed antibodies against them, got hits to half, and at that point I think pharma starts to realize, okay, there are actually signs of life here and this might actually work in some of our programs. Antibodies is maybe a more challenging domain than other structural prediction problems.

items.question: Why did you decide to build a web server for Chai 1 so close to its release?
items.object: The web server for Chai 1
items.answer: We were like, “Oh man, we really want to be the first to put this out.” We were one week out. items.question: How did you think about the scope of Chai's protein design work as you moved toward Chai 2?
items.object: Chai's approach to protein design and antibody generation
items.answer: After that we set our sights on design, and really what we were thinking is we kind of always had antibodies in mind. We thought of this as the most tractable problem. The nice thing with proteins is you have this beautiful sequence representation, and there's already a lot of research done in how do you autoregressively generate sequences? This sequence generation problem is well studied. We were thinking, what's a nice area to apply sequence generation to in the bio space? It's pretty natural to do linear sequences of amino acids. We start working on design. We don't really pigeonhole ourselves into one therapeutic area. We tried to tackle this problem very generally. Can we design many proteins? Can we design antibodies? Can we scaffold regular complexes? Really just take a holistic view on how do you design proteins in general? That eventually led to the Chai 2 model. That was our first flagship design model, and that's where the Chai 2 paper and our bold target discovery project came in. We designed antibodies to 50 targets for that paper, got binders to about half of them, with I think on average around a 20% hit rate for binding.

items.question: How do you think about the background you need to work on AI for biology?
items.object: The expertise needed to work on AI for biology
items.answer: All this bio stuff sounds kind of scary, atoms, tokens, amino acids. At the end of the day, my background personally is theoretical computer science. That's what I spent all of my earlier years doing, transitioning to this pretty late in my PhD. But I think the background that you need is really similar to the background that you need for any other field of machine learning. There are all these domain-specific things that you learn about. One analogy or anecdote I like to say is people think you can't work on AI bio unless you're a biologist, but it's kind of like you can't work on video models unless you're a director or something. There are all these super domain-specific things, like to understand lighting and video, things like that, but at the end of the day these are just machine learning problems, and they're all solved the same way.

items.question: How do you think about representing protein design in Chai 2’s all-atom diffusion model?
items.object: Chai 2’s all-atom approach to protein design
items.answer: What we've disclosed about Chai 2 is it is an all-atom diffusion model. We're trying to predict atoms in 3D space still, but we're doing it in such a way that the model actually has the ability to design atoms, place them, decide which atoms actually are there. One way to represent an amino acid, a protein token, is by which atoms are present. In the Chai 2 case, we were just predicting, all right, show the model, let the model just kind of pick what atoms it wants to keep, and then map that back to what amino acids there are.

items.question: What did you take away from validating Chai 2’s protein predictions with cryo-EM?
items.object: Cryo-EM validation of Chai 2 protein predictions
items.answer: I remember there's this really funny anecdote. In Chai 2, we actually did that. We took some of the proteins that the model predicted and ran cryo-EM, and we got the results back and we're like, wait, the results look wrong, because we had overlaid the prediction over the point cloud, the electron cloud, and we didn't see any difference. The point being, we're getting to the point now where these structure prediction models are within a few angstroms or less of the actual atomic positions that you validate. In this case it was a 0.33 angstrom error, which is one-third the width of an atom, and we were like, this can't even be right. Clearly they just sent us back the wrong design.

items.question: Why do you try not to distinguish between hit discovery and lead optimization when developing Chai’s models?
items.object: The distinction between hit discovery and lead optimization in AI drug development
items.answer: Part of the reason why we think of it that way is because the initial molecules are usually not good enough to be drugs. Really, we're kind of at the inflection point now. We're seeing this internally at Chai, where the models are getting pretty close to producing molecules that could eventually, or are very close to, drugs. We try not to make too much of a distinction between hit discovery, lead optimization, all of the different parts of this preclinical pipeline. Our north star is to produce drug-like molecules straight out of the models. Of course this is going to be hard and there are going to be tons of roadblocks. You need to be able to prompt the model to do this; you need the whole RL stack to learn different properties, things along those lines. But I think it's very achievable.

items.question: Why do you see parsing biological structure data as a difficult engineering problem?
items.object: Parsing biological structure data as an obstacle to engineering drug discovery
items.answer: Just when you're actually parsing, first of all, file formats for biologists. They just don't care. There are standardized file formats. Are they the best? I don't really know. But there's also a lot of information that you want to pack in: I have this structure, here are the people who solved it, this is the method I used to solve it. There's a lot going on. Depending on the method that you use to figure out what this 3D structure is, you might have multiple copies of that structure. Part of it might not have really been resolved, or you're like, it could be here, it could be there; I'm just going to give you both options. The actual parsing problem on the engineering side of working with this type of data is really difficult.

items.question: Why do you favor a simple, principled approach to parsing biological structure data even with capable language models available?
items.object: A simple, principled approach to code for parsing biological structure data
items.answer: They don't know all the edge cases often. This is more back to just a simplicity approach. LMs are very good, I will absolutely give you that. Then you're thinking about, do I really want to—should this function have 20 special cases, or should we be really principled in how we approach this? How opinionated should we be in how we do this? We want a strategy that's easy enough for humans to understand, and when we're reading through the codebase, we really need to know what's going on here, what are the potential problems. Sometimes that comes down to looking at examples.

items.question: How do you think about the compute bottlenecks that make engineering optimization important for a Chai 1-type model?
items.object: Compute bottlenecks and optimization in Chai 1-type models
items.answer: We can go back to a Chai 1-type model. In that case we're following the Fold 2/3 architecture, and there, rather than doing attention over a normal sequence representation, you're loosely doing attention over this pair representation. You can think of this as a sequence of length L squared rather than typically length L. If you're doing attention over that, the way that you actually batch this up ends up being L cubed. Now you're in a pretty heavy compute regime. The amount of flops that you're putting into every token stays pretty high. The memory bandwidth overhead of transferring that from SRAM to whatever, that's a real bottleneck in these architectures. Even something as simple as a layer norm can take a long time; that can be a significant amount of the compute that you're using. On our side we've spent a lot of time optimizing it and taking engineering very seriously so these operations are at least better. We're always looking at how new chips perform compared to older versions. Sometimes that's different for training versus inference, and of course Neil knows this really well.

items.question: How do you think about applying general machine-learning approaches to protein modeling at Chai?
items.object: Chai's first-principles approach to protein modeling
items.answer: We're pretty first-principles people, the whole research team at Chai. Except for me and Kevin, we're the only people with, quote, bio background, even still we're pretty far removed. We try to look at every problem as a core ML problem. We try to think of what's the analog in other spaces. Even for image models, CNNs were built to process images, so images should be looked at in patches. That was the nice inductive bias there. Then people are like, well, you can just tokenize this thing and throw it into a transformer, and it's going to work, and it did end up working, even on a relatively small data set. For proteins in particular it is really hard. There's not as much structural data. There's a ton of sequence data, and that's one of the unlocks for ESM working. You can get that to just run on a transformer. If you try to do the same thing with experimental structure data, good luck.

items.question: How do you think about the architectural tradeoffs of triangle layers in protein models?
items.object: Triangle layers in protein-model architectures
items.answer: I think these layers are pretty costly, and that kind of limits what you can do with the architectures. They're not only costly in terms of compute, they're just not efficient on modern GPUs either. You have small hidden dimensions, large sequence dimensions; it's exactly the opposite of what GPUs are designed to process. One takeaway from triangle layers is you're trading off parameters for compute, in that sense. That's one mental model for thinking about this.

items.question: How would you like to see talent allocated differently across the economy?
items.object: Talent allocation across biology, software, and other fields
items.answer:
I'm going to take a much more abstract answer to that, which is talent obscurity. There's a lot of smart people going and working on LLMs. There's a lot of people working and becoming software engineers for SaaS, but not that many smart people go and work on bio. I didn't work on bio in high school because I was like, oh, I could pick up my computer and program apps, but if I want to work on bio I have to go study and get good grades in school and maybe get a PhD or whatever. Maybe that's one reason for it. Another reason is a lot of this stuff is really obscure. We threw around a lot of big words during this podcast. You can't really visualize the things. It's one of the things we care a lot about at Chai: how do we make the whole thing feel visual on our website and in the product? Part of the reason we're here is I think more people should realize you don't need to have a super specialist bio background to contribute to this computationally.

I think a lot about talent flows and where talent goes in the economy. In the '90s everyone was flowing to talent, and since the 2000s people have been flowing to tech. Big tech ate up a lot of the talent until a few years ago, and now maybe LLMs and the big AI labs are eating up a lot of the good talent. At the meta level, how do you allocate talent better? Selfishly, I want more talent going into bio. We probably want more talent going into manufacturing and physical-world things and these other problems that the US has. I think communicating that better would be the thing that, if I had a megaphone to talk to everyone, I would try to do.

items.question: Why do you see machine learning for biology as such a compelling field for researchers to work in?
items.object: Machine learning for biology as a research field
items.answer: For me, the biggest takeaway is that the field is actually working. Not only does it have commercial traction, but the research is actually showing signs of life. It's not even just showing signs of life; the signs of life have been showed. We're in a place where the models work. They're delivering value, and there's still tons of really interesting research problems to solve. There's a lot more low-hanging fruit in this field than there would be in other fields. The amount of impact that you can have, especially as a researcher, is unmatched in this field. We're all very mission-driven, but even if you're not, it's a lot of fun puzzles to solve. There's a 3D geometry angle. If you like diffusion models, there's a million problems to solve in that regard. We have this LLM-looking trunk in Chai 1. So much of core machine learning is touched by these problems. Although we've made a ton of progress, there's still a lot to be done. I think it's one of the most interesting fields to be working in, while also having some of the largest impact on humanity.
